# Equality rigidity for distal overlap and compact stability

This is an ordinary continuous theorem. Its inputs are the proved distal
truncation inequality and the ordinary minimal-maximal-depth rigidity
in `candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c`. The latter
uses the classical equality case of Gruenbaum and proves the passage
from equality of maximal depth to a simplex. No mixed-integer equality
classification is assumed here.

## 1. Sharp equality theorem

Let D>=2, let K be a convex body in R^D of volume V, and let D+1 closed
halfspaces H_i cover K. Suppose every cap mass

    A_i=vol_D(K intersect H_i)

is positive. Write

    gamma=(D/(D+1))^D,    a=min_i A_i>0,
    r=D+1-1/gamma.

Then

    E=sum_i A_i-V-r a>=0.                              (1)

Equality holds if and only if K is a simplex and, after indexing its
vertices, H_i are exactly its D+1 canonical centroid vertex caps.
In particular equality forces

    A_1=...=A_(D+1)=a=gamma V.

Repeated original halfspaces are permitted in the hypothesis; equality
forces the D+1 canonical halfspaces to be distinct. There is no normal
rank, concurrency, smoothness, or initial simpliciality assumption.

## 2. The equality chain in distal trimming

Nonnegativity in (1) is the distal-truncation theorem, proved in
`candidate cd833c78fb705a2e`. We include its
exact equality implications. Write H_i={x:u_i.x>=b_i}, with u_i!=0.
For every i with A_i>a, choose t_i>=b_i such that

    vol_D(K intersect {u_i.x>t_i})=A_i-a.

These thresholds exist by continuous cap tails; strict versus closed
outer boundaries changes no volume. Define

    R_i=K intersect {u_i.x>t_i}       when A_i>a,
    R_i=empty                         when A_i=a,
    K'=K intersect intersection_(i:A_i>a){u_i.x<=t_i}.

Then K minus K' is exactly the union of the R_i, and every original
cap has mass at most a in K'. If E=0, then

    V-sum_i vol(R_i)=V-sum_i(A_i-a)=a/gamma>0.

Thus K' is a full-dimensional convex body with

    vol(K')>=a/gamma.

Its centroid belongs to one of the original covering caps. Ordinary
Gruenbaum bounds that cap below by gamma vol(K'), whereas its mass is
at most a. Therefore

    vol(K')=a/gamma.                                   (2)

Also equality holds in the union bound for the R_i:

    vol(union_i R_i)=sum_i vol(R_i).                    (3)

In a finite measurable family this implies every pairwise intersection
R_i intersect R_j has volume zero: integrate the nonnegative excess of
the sum of indicators over the indicator of the union.

At every point of K', some original cap contains that point and has
K'-mass at most a. The maximum normalized halfspace depth of K' is
therefore at most a/vol(K')=gamma. Gruenbaum at its centroid gives the
opposite bound. The archived ordinary depth-rigidity theorem now shows
that K' is a D-simplex. Denote its centroid by g.

## 3. All original caps must be the canonical caps of K'

Consider the indices I_g for which g belongs to H_i. Gruenbaum and
(2) give

    vol(K' intersect H_i)=a=gamma vol(K'),    i in I_g.

The boundary of each such cap passes through g. If g lay strictly
inside H_i, moving its boundary to g would remove a positive-volume
slab in a ball about g inside K'. The resulting centroid cap already
has mass at least gamma vol(K'), contradicting the displayed equality.

The classical equality case says that K' is a pyramid with its apex
on the included side and base parallel to this equality cut. In a
simplex, such an apex is a vertex and its base is the opposite facet.
Consequently every H_i with i in I_g is one of the canonical halfspaces

    {lambda_j>=1/(D+1)},                               (4)

where lambda_0,...,lambda_D are the barycentric affine functions of K'.
These are actual ambient halfspaces, not only almost-everywhere traces:
the equality plane cuts the interior of the full-dimensional simplex,
so its affine hyperplane and orientation are uniquely determined.

Because the family is finite, the caps not containing g miss an entire
neighborhood of g. The caps indexed by I_g must therefore cover a ball
about g. A proper subset of the distinct halfspaces in (4) cannot do so.
Indeed, for a proper index set J, choose barycentric increments delta_j
negative on J and positive on its nonempty complement, with sum zero.
The point with coordinates 1/(D+1)+epsilon delta_j is interior for
sufficiently small epsilon>0, tends to g, and misses every selected cap.
Thus I_g contains all D+1 distinct canonical halfspaces. There are only
D+1 original caps, so every original cap is canonical for K', with
exactly one copy of each, and every cap has K'-mass a.

## 4. Positive trimming would create an impossible facet

Suppose some R_i has positive volume. Convex K has a volume-null
boundary, and finitely many hyperplanes are volume-null. Thus one can
choose

    x in int(K) intersect R_i

which lies on none of the other cutting hyperplanes. Equation (3)
implies x cannot belong to any R_j with j!=i: if it did, the strict
outer inequalities and x in int(K) would give an open ball in their
intersection, contradicting its zero volume. Consequently

    u_j.x<t_j        for every other actual cut j.

Because g belongs to int(K'), it also lies in int(K) and strictly
satisfies every actual retained inequality, including u_i.g<t_i.
The segment from g to x crosses u_i.z=t_i at a point z in int(K).
At that crossing all other retained inequalities are still strict.
A small ball about z therefore lies in int(K) and strictly inside all
other retained sides. Locally, K' is exactly the intersection of that
ball with {u_i.x<=t_i}. Hence

    K' intersect {u_i.x=t_i}

is a supporting face of dimension D-1: it contains a relatively open
(D-1)-disk. It is a genuine facet of the simplex K'.

But Section 3 identifies u_i as a positive multiple of the gradient
of one barycentric coordinate of K'. Maximizing that coordinate on a
simplex exposes only its single corresponding vertex. Its supporting
face has dimension zero, contradicting D-1>=1. Thus no R_i has positive
volume. By its definition, this means no A_i exceeds a, so no cut was
imposed and K'=K. Sections 2--3 prove the asserted simplex and cap
classification.

Conversely the canonical centroid vertex caps of a simplex have mass
gamma V, cover the simplex, and give equality in (1). This completes
both directions.

The same argument gives a slightly stronger profile equality statement.
For any D+1-cap cover, even allowing zero original cap masses, and any
alpha>0, equality in

    sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+ + alpha/gamma=V

holds if and only if K is a simplex, all original caps are its distinct
canonical centroid vertex caps, and alpha=A_i=gamma V for every i.
Indeed the equality chain now starts with
`V-sum_i(A_i-alpha)_+=alpha/gamma>0`; replacing a by alpha in Sections
2--3 gives a simplex K' and all D+1 canonical original cap traces of
mass alpha. In particular no original mass is less than alpha. The
pairwise-disjoint distal-piece and impossible-facet argument in Section
4 rules out every A_i>alpha. Thus no cut was imposed and all masses
equal alpha. Conversely the displayed simplex configuration has the
asserted equality. The strict premise alpha>0 is essential to this
version, since an exact two-cap partition with extra empty caps has
positive-part equality at alpha=0.

## 5. The one-dimensional exception

In dimension D=1, K is an interval and gamma_1=1/2, so the two-cap
coefficient is r=0. With both cap masses positive, equality is exactly
zero overlap volume. After exchanging indices, the two traces must
partition the interval at any interior point c:

    K intersect {x<=c},    K intersect {x>=c}.

To check this classification, same-oriented halfspaces can cover the
interval only if one contains the entire interval, which gives positive
overlap with the other positive cap. Opposite-oriented proper caps
have zero overlap while covering precisely when their thresholds agree
at an interior point. Thus equality need not occur at the interval
midpoint, and the two masses need not coincide. In Section 4 an interval
endpoint has dimension D-1=0, so the facet-versus-vertex contradiction
correctly fails. No claim of higher-dimensional rigidity is made for D=1.

## 6. A compact stability consequence with attained modulus

Fix D>=2, tau>0, and eta>0. There exists epsilon(D,tau,eta)>0 with
the following property. For a body and D+1-cap cover as in Section 1,
assume

    min_i A_i>=tau V,    E<=epsilon(D,tau,eta)V.         (5)

Choose ANY maximum-volume inscribed D-simplex of K and map its
vertices affinely to the standard simplex

    T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_D).

Write K* for the transformed body. After normalizing transformed cap
normals to length one and clipping only irrelevant full-cap offsets as
below, the conclusions are

    d_H(K*,T)<eta,
    |A_i/V-gamma|<eta for every i,

and, up to permutation, all D+1 unit-normal/offset pairs lie within
eta of the canonical cap pairs of T. This is a qualitative modulus
attained on a compact bad set; no rate or uniformity in D is claimed.

Here are all required compactness details. The maximum-volume inscribed
simplex exists because its determinant volume is continuous on the
compact set of D+1 vertex tuples. Its volume is positive because K has
interior. After the normalization, replacing the j-th standard simplex
vertex by x in K* gives an inscribed simplex of volume
`|lambda_j(x)|/D!`. Maximality implies every |lambda_j(x)|<=1. Hence

    T subset K* subset Q_D={x:|lambda_j(x)|<=1 for all j},

where Q_D is a fixed compact polytope contained in the radius-sqrt(D)
ball, since its coordinate functions x_i=lambda_i lie in [-1,1].
Every inscribed D-simplex of K* has volume at most 1/D!, and K* has
volume at least 1/D!.

The class C of all convex bodies with these inclusions and maximal
inscribed simplex volume at most 1/D! is Hausdorff compact. Uniformly
bounded support functions are uniformly Lipschitz, giving a convergent
subsequence by Arzela--Ascoli. The two inclusions persist, and every
simplex in the limit is approximated vertexwise by simplices in the
sequence, so the maximal-simplex condition persists too. Every limit
still contains the full-dimensional standard simplex.

Set R=D+1, strictly larger than the containing radius. Represent each
cap by {x:u_i.x>=b_i}, |u_i|=1. A positive cap has b_i<R. If b_i<-R,
replace b_i by -R; this changes only a full trace and preserves that
trace exactly for every body in C. Thus all cap parameters lie in the
compact set `(S^(D-1) times [-R,R])^(D+1)`.

Volumes and all cap masses are continuous under these body and parameter
limits: the indicators converge almost everywhere except on the null
boundary of the limiting full-dimensional body and its cap hyperplanes,
and a fixed ball dominates the integrands. Denominators are at least
1/D!. The covering property is closed, since any point of a limiting
body is a limit of points in the approximating bodies, and a subsequence
lies in one fixed closed cap. The positive minimum condition in (5)
is therefore also closed. This gives a compact normalized covered class
C_tau, possibly empty.

Equality E=0 on this compact class forces K* to be a simplex with
canonical caps, by Sections 1--4. Since it contains T and every
inscribed simplex has volume at most 1/D!, that simplex equals T.
Its canonical unit parameters are

    (e_i,1/(D+1)),       1<=i<=D,
    (-1_D/sqrt(D),-sqrt(D)/(D+1)).

Define the discrepancy as the maximum of Hausdorff distance to T,
the D+1 deviations |A_i/V-gamma|, and the minimum over all permutations
of the largest Euclidean parameter distance to the listed canonical
pairs. This is a continuous function on C_tau. Its closed subset on
which discrepancy>=eta is compact. If nonempty, the continuous
nonnegative E/V attains a strictly positive minimum there, since any
zero would have discrepancy zero by the equality theorem. Take epsilon
to be half that minimum. If the bad set is empty, take epsilon=1.
These choices prove (5) and all its conclusions.

Every choice of a maximizing simplex lies in this same compact class;
no continuous choice of normalization is assumed. The positive lower
cap fraction tau prevents zero-cap limits and is retained explicitly.
Neither this ordinary normalization nor the individual distal cuts
are applied independently to a mixed-integer convex body here.
